title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 12
topics: A time you taught someone something
Teaching, learning and who does it best

questions: Are you good at explaining things to other people, would you say?
Has anyone ever asked you to explain how to use a phone or an app? How did it go?
When someone explains something badly to you, what do they usually get wrong?
Were you the kind of student who explained things to classmates, or the one asking?
Do you think you'll need to explain things more or less in your future work?
What do you like doing in your free time these days?
How did you first get into that? Did someone introduce you to it?
Is it something you prefer doing alone or with other people?
Is there a hobby you had as a child that you've completely dropped?
Is there anything you'd love to take up if you had more time or money?

part2.title: Describe a time you taught something to another person.
bullets: who you taught and what you taught them
why you were the one teaching them
how you went about explaining it
what difficulties came up while you were teaching
part2.explain: and explain how you felt about the experience, and whether the person actually learned it in the end.
followups: Would you say you're a patient teacher?
Has that person taught you anything in return?
Would you enjoy teaching as a full-time job?

part3.q: What separates a good explanation from a bad one?
followups: Can you think of someone who explains things brilliantly — what do they do?
Is it mostly about the words, or something else?

part3.q: Some people know a subject deeply but can't teach it at all. Why does that happen?
followups: So is teaching a separate skill from knowing?
Can that gap be trained away?

part3.q: Students often say they understand a topic better when a classmate explains it than when the teacher does. How would you account for that?
followups: Should schools build on that deliberately?
Are there risks in letting students teach each other?

part3.q: People say the best way to learn something is to teach it. Do you think that's actually true?
followups: Why would teaching deepen the teacher's own understanding?
Does it work for every kind of knowledge?

part3.q: With video tutorials available on almost any topic, what can a live teacher still offer that a recording cannot?
followups: Will that advantage shrink as technology improves?
Does it depend on the age of the learner?

part3.q: How much respect do teachers get in your country, compared with doctors or engineers?
followups: Why do you think that difference exists?
Has it changed within your lifetime?

part3.q: In some countries teaching attracts top graduates; in others it's seen as a fallback career. What drives that difference between societies?
followups: Is it mainly about salary, or something deeper?
What would actually change it?

part3.q: Do you think everyone should have to teach something at some point in their lives?
followups: What would people gain from it?
Who would you exempt, if anyone?

part3.q: Parents are often described as a child's first teachers. Is what they teach more important than what schools teach?
followups: What do children learn only at home?
What happens when home and school teach conflicting things?

part3.q: If machines eventually deliver most instruction, what should human teachers spend their time doing instead?
followups: Is that a better use of a teacher than delivering content?
Would you have wanted that kind of schooling yourself?

fc: The Part 2 teaching story holds its sequence — what was taught, the method, the difficulty, the outcome — without doubling back to add forgotten pieces.
Describes a process fluently: explaining how you taught something is itself an explanation, and the examiner hears you sequencing steps in real time.
In Part 3, develops the society-level questions (teacher status, top graduates) past one sentence without needing the printed follow-ups.
Repairs smoothly when a comparison gets tangled — "or maybe a better way to put it is…" — and keeps going.
Sounds like thinking aloud, not reciting: the 'learning by teaching' question gets a considered answer, not a proverb repeated back.
lr: Teaching vocabulary used with precision: break something down, walk someone through it, pick it up, sink in, hands-on, learn by doing.
Distinguishes teach, explain, demonstrate, coach and train — five different acts this test invites you to confuse.
Natural collocations: "grasp the concept", "lose patience", "a steep learning curve", "tailor the explanation to the person".
Hobby talk in Part 1 sounds real: "I dabbled in it for a year", "I'm completely hooked", "it fell by the wayside when exams started".
Abstract Part 3 language arrives without strain: prestige, vocation, one-size-fits-all, rote learning, mentorship.
gra: Past narrative plus process language in Part 2: "first I showed her…, then I got her to try it herself while I watched".
Causatives handled correctly — "I had him repeat it", "I got her to practise", "I let him make the mistake" — the natural grammar of teaching stories.
Comparatives carry the Part 3 contrasts: "far better paid than", "nowhere near as respected as", "the younger the learner, the more that matters".
Hypotheticals for the policy questions: "If teaching paid what engineering pays, the queue would look very different."
Concession without collapse: "Even though a video can be replayed endlessly, it can't notice that you've stopped following."
pron: Instruction sequences get natural list intonation — rising through the steps, falling on the last — so the process is audible, not monotone.
Stress lands on the contrast the question sets up: "knowing something and teaching it are completely different skills."
The word 'taught' comes out as /tɔːt/, clearly distinct from 'thought' — this cue card makes you say it constantly.
Patience words often mispronounced — patience, thorough, encourage — are stressed on the right syllable.
Pace drops slightly when explaining the difficult moment in the story, which reads as reflection rather than hesitation.

band9.part1: Answer the question, then plant one detail that proves the answer is yours. For "Has anyone ever asked you to explain how to use a phone or an app?" a Band 9 answer is specific and slightly wry: "Constantly — I'm my mother's unofficial tech support. Last month it was video calls; the breakthrough came when I stopped demonstrating and just let her press the buttons herself while I sat on my hands." Real detail, natural humour, and it already contains an idea about teaching.
part2: Open with the pairing — who you taught, what you taught them, and the relationship, in one or two sentences: "I ended up teaching my younger cousin to ride a bicycle the summer he turned eight."
Explain why it fell to you — the second bullet is easy to skip; a line like "his parents had tried and given up, and I was the one he didn't feel embarrassed in front of" adds real texture.
Describe your method concretely — what you actually did first, next, and after that, so the examiner hears a process rather than a summary.
Give the difficulty its own moment — the point where it wasn't working, what the learner felt, and what you changed; this bullet is where the story earns its interest.
Show the turning point — the specific moment it clicked, described visually: "he was ten metres ahead before he realised I'd let go."
Close on both halves of the explain line — how the experience felt for you, and an honest verdict on whether the learning stuck.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Some people know a subject deeply but can't teach it at all. Why does that happen?
framework: Answer: name the mechanism directly — experts forget what it was like not to know; the steps that confuse a beginner have become invisible to them.
Explain: develop it — once knowledge becomes automatic, the expert can no longer see its parts, so they skip the exact links a novice needs and mistake speed for clarity.

Example: ground it — a brilliant mathematician who says 'it's obvious' at the precise moment it isn't, versus a slightly older student who struggled with the same point last year and remembers where it bites.
Alternative view: concede genuinely — some experts do teach superbly, usually because they stayed curious about their own early confusion, which suggests the gap is a habit, not a law.
Evaluate: land it — expertise tells you what to teach, but memory of difficulty tells you how; the best teachers keep one foot in the learner's world, and that, not knowledge, is the scarce skill.

mistakes.title: Choosing something too trivial to teach
mistakes.detail: "I taught my friend to save a contact on his phone" is over in twenty seconds and offers no difficulties to describe. Pick something with stages and a struggle — swimming, cooking a dish, a grammar point — so all four bullets have material.

mistakes.title: Narrating the subject instead of the teaching
mistakes.detail: Candidates who taught chess explain the rules of chess to the examiner. The card wants the teaching — your method, the learner's confusion, what you changed — not a lecture on the content itself.

mistakes.title: Skipping the difficulties bullet
mistakes.detail: "He learned it very fast, no problem" throws away the best part of the story and usually leaves the candidate stranded at ninety seconds. The struggle is what makes the ending mean something; keep it in even if you have to remember hard.

mistakes.title: Claiming teaching talent with no evidence
mistakes.detail: "I am very good at explaining things" in Part 1, followed by a vague Part 2 with no method in it, contradicts itself. Show the skill through the story — the examiner scores what you demonstrate, not what you declare.

mistakes.title: Reciting a 'technology in education' essay
mistakes.detail: The video-tutorial and machine-instruction questions sit next to a well-worn memorised topic, and examiners hear the pivot instantly. These questions ask what humans still add — answer that, specifically.

mistakes.title: Answering the teacher-status question with salary alone
mistakes.detail: "Teachers are respected less because they earn less" is one cause presented as the whole answer. Band 8–9 responses touch prestige, history, or how a society talks about the profession — then weigh which factor drives the others.

mistakes.title: Using 'teach' for everything
mistakes.detail: The topic hands you a family of verbs — explain, show, demonstrate, coach, guide, walk through — and using only 'teach' for two minutes flattens your Lexical Resource score on a test built to showcase it.

mistakes.title: Saying 'learn someone something'
mistakes.detail: A classic confusion this cue card exposes: you teach someone, they learn from you. "I learned my brother to swim" is exactly the kind of repeated, noticeable error that caps Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

mistakes.title: Dodging the 'should everyone teach?' question
mistakes.detail: It's an opinion question, and "it depends on the person" with nothing after it is a non-answer. Take a side, give the gain — empathy, humility, clearer thinking — and name your exceptions if you want nuance.

mistakes.title: Rushing the process description
mistakes.detail: Explaining your teaching method is where this Part 2 shows fluency and sequencing language — first, then, once she'd got that. Candidates who compress it to "I just showed him how" waste the card's whole design.
